1-01: In ascending order, if the middle value is smaller than the target, every value to its left is also too small. The reverse applies to the right half when the middle value is too large. In [4, 1, 3], searching for 4 by comparing with 1 can discard the half containing 4.
1-02: A resize from capacity c copies c elements, and c grows as 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on. These copy costs form a geometric series below 2n over n appends. Adding n ordinary writes gives O(n) total work, so each append costs O(1) amortized even though one resize can take O(n).
1-03: A linked list has O(n) positional lookup because you follow links, while an array indexes in O(1). Scattered node allocations can also hurt cache locality. Inserting after a node you already hold is O(1), but finding that node first can cost O(n).
1-04: Scan left to right and push every opening bracket. For a closing bracket, reject if the stack is empty or its top is the wrong matching opener. Otherwise pop. Accept only if the stack is empty at the end. An initial closer is rejected immediately.
1-05: Enqueue by pushing onto the input stack. Dequeue from the output stack, first moving every input item to output if output is empty. This reversal puts the oldest item on top. Each element crosses stacks at most once, so a transfer-heavy dequeue can be O(n), but operations are O(1) amortized.
1-06: In a min-heap every parent is at most its children, so the root is a minimum. Siblings and unrelated subtrees are not sorted relative to each other. If you remove the root from consideration, the smallest remaining value is the smaller of its children, assuming a child exists. Ties can occur.
1-07: Sift down only the internal nodes, starting at the bottom. About half the nodes are leaves and do no work, about a quarter can move down at most one level, and progressively fewer can move far. Summing O(nh / 2^h) across heights h gives O(n) total work.
1-08: Separate chaining keeps colliding keys together in a bucket structure. Open addressing keeps all keys in the array and probes other slots. As the load factor grows, chains get longer or empty slots get harder to find. Resizing spreads the keys out and reduces expected lookup work.
1-09: BFS uses a queue and expands a graph layer by layer, which suits shortest paths measured in edges. DFS uses a stack or recursion and follows a branch before backtracking, which suits checking reachability and, with visitation states, detecting directed cycles.
1-10: BFS visits all nodes at distance d before expanding nodes at distance d+1. So when an unweighted node is first reached, no shorter path can remain undiscovered. Mark nodes when enqueueing, including the source, so multiple neighbors do not enqueue the same node or replace its first parent.
1-11: A trie follows the letters of a query, so finding the prefix node and enumerating its descendants is natural. A hash set is simpler for exact membership and has expected O(1) table access after hashing the word. A trie may use substantial memory for nodes and child links, especially with sparse branching.
1-12: Give each vertex its own set. For each undirected edge (u, v), compare find(u) with find(v). If they match, an earlier path already connects the endpoints and this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise union their sets. Path compression and union by size or rank keep operations nearly constant amortized.
1-13: A stable sort preserves the order of equal keys. For example, sort employee records by name first, then stably sort by department. Employees in each department remain alphabetized, so department becomes the primary key and name remains the secondary key.
1-14: With sorted, distinct input and the first element as pivot, each partition leaves an empty side and a side of size n−1. The total partition work is n+(n−1)+…+1, or O(n²). Choosing a random pivot reduces the chance of consistently bad partitions and gives expected O(n log n) time.
1-15: Typical array merge sort uses an O(n) temporary buffer for merging. In-place array quicksort partitions within the original array and uses stack space, typically O(log n) for balanced partitions but O(n) in the naive worst case. Linked-list merge sort can merge by relinking nodes instead of allocating an array buffer.
1-16: Start both pointers at the head. While fast and fast.next exist, advance slow one step and fast two. At termination slow is at the middle, or the second middle for an even-length list. To choose the first middle, stop one iteration earlier when fast.next.next is absent.
1-17: Move slow one link and fast two. Inside a cycle fast gains one position per iteration modulo the cycle length, so they meet. After meeting, move one pointer back to the head, then advance both one step at a time. Their next meeting is the cycle entry because the initial offset equals the remaining distance modulo the cycle length.
1-18: Compute the sum of the first k elements and initialize the maximum to that sum. Slide one position at a time, subtracting the element that leaves and adding the one that enters. Update the maximum each time. This takes O(n) instead of O(nk), including for arrays of negative values.
1-19: With zero-based indexing, let P[0]=0 and P[i+1]=P[i]+a[i]. P[r+1] includes values from index 0 through r, and P[l] includes those before l. Therefore the inclusive sum from l through r is P[r+1]−P[l], O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
1-20: Maintain a min-heap with at most k elements. Insert until full, then replace the minimum only if a new item is larger. The heap contains the largest k seen so far. It takes O(k) memory and O(n log k) time for k≥2 (O(n) when k=1), instead of storing and sorting all n items.
2-01: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and requires every key column to be non-NULL. A UNIQUE constraint enforces uniqueness for a candidate field but does not by itself always impose NOT NULL. How many NULL entries are allowed by UNIQUE depends on the database dialect and constraint options.
2-02: Enrollments.student_id can reference Students.id. The foreign key prevents a non-NULL enrollment reference to a student that does not exist. Updates or deletes of the parent follow the configured action, such as reject, cascade or set NULL. Use NOT NULL if every enrollment must identify a student.
2-03: INNER JOIN returns only rows satisfying the join predicate on both sides. A customer with no orders yields no matching pair, so it disappears. Starting from Customers with LEFT JOIN Orders keeps that customer, filling order columns with NULL.
2-04: WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups afterward. Example: `SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM Sales WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000`. This groups paid rows, then retains only regions above the total threshold.
2-05: COUNT(*) counts rows even if all selected columns are NULL. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is non-NULL. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts the different non-NULL values in that column. For values [7, 7, NULL], the three results are 3, 2 and 1.
2-06: Comparisons such as column = NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN, even when column is NULL. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Use column IS NULL to find missing values and column IS NOT NULL to find present ones. TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN follow SQL's three-valued logic.
2-07: NOT IN is effectively a series of inequality tests. If no value matches but the subquery includes NULL, the result can be UNKNOWN and WHERE discards the row. A correlated NOT EXISTS tests whether a matching row actually exists. If outer NULLs should also be excluded, add an explicit outer IS NOT NULL predicate.
2-08: A typical B-tree on (department, salary) is ordered by department first, then salary within a department. It efficiently supports a department filter or department plus salary range. A salary-only filter may need to scan a large part of the index or use a separate salary index. Some engines support optimizations such as skip scans.
2-09: Every affected index must be maintained as rows are inserted, deleted or its indexed values change. Index pages also consume disk and cache space. A low-selectivity filter that returns many rows may be faster with a table scan than with numerous index lookups, so measure query plans and write costs.
2-10: A logical plan describes what to compute, such as filtering and joining relations. A physical plan specifies how to execute it, such as scanning a table or index and choosing nested-loop, hash or merge joins. The optimizer uses available indexes, statistics and estimated work to choose among equivalent implementations.
2-11: Suppose student_id determines department_id, which determines department_name. Storing department_name in every student row duplicates a fact and can leave inconsistent names after a rename. Keep Students(student_id, department_id) and Departments(department_id, department_name) so the department's name is updated once.
2-12: Create Students and Courses with their own primary keys. Add Enrollments(student_id, course_id) with foreign keys to both. The pair can be its primary key to prevent duplicate enrollment, or use a separate ID and put a UNIQUE constraint on the pair. Store relationship-specific data such as enrollment date there.
2-13: Perform the debit and credit inside one transaction. If credit fails, roll back so the debit is undone too. Commit only after both changes and any related checks succeed. Atomicity means the transaction takes effect as a whole or not at all.
2-14: If both sessions read 100 and write 110 after adding 10, one increment disappears. Use a single UPDATE balance = balance + 10, where the database handles the concurrent change, or lock the row before reading with SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside the transaction and then write the computed result.
2-15: A dirty read sees another transaction's uncommitted change. A non-repeatable read rereads a row and gets a changed or missing version after another transaction commits. A phantom read reruns a predicate query and sees the set of matching rows change, such as when a new matching row is inserted.
2-16: OFFSET counts positions in the current result. Insertions or deletions before that position shift the next page, so a row may be repeated or skipped. Cursor pagination filters after the last displayed sort key, with a unique tie-breaker such as (created_at, id). Changes to ordering keys can still affect traversal.
2-17: GROUP BY department with AVG(salary) returns one summary row per department. AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) adds the department average to each employee row without collapsing rows. Use the window version when each employee and the comparison value must remain visible.
2-18: A feed that repeatedly shows answer counts can store a count on each question to avoid recounting its answers on every read. The cost is that every addition and deletion must update both representations. Plan for atomic updates, reconciliation or tolerable lag if they drift.
2-19: A relational design might use Questions and Answers tables with foreign keys and joins. A document design could embed a small, bounded list of answers or store them separately when they grow independently. Document stores allow varied fields, but validation and indexing still matter. Model around query patterns and consistency needs.
2-20: A placeholder binds an input as a value rather than adding characters to the SQL program. Quotes or comments in a user value cannot then change the statement structure. Table names, column names and sort directions usually are not bindable values. Choose those from a predefined allowlist.
3-01: For Java object references, == tests whether both references identify the same object. String.equals tests whether their character contents match. Identical literals are often interned and can refer to the same object, making == appear to work until the equal string is created from input or another allocation.
3-02: If a.equals(b) is true, both objects must return the same hashCode. HashMap uses the hash to narrow the search and then uses equality to distinguish keys. Different keys may have the same hash without being equal. Correct equality still separates them, though many collisions can make lookup slower.
3-03: A map places a key based on the hash at insertion. If a field used by hashCode changes, a later lookup may search a different bucket. A field used in equals can likewise change which lookups match. Use immutable keys or keep fields used in equality stable while the key is stored.
3-04: ArrayList offers constant-time indexed reads, efficient sequential traversal and amortized constant-time append. LinkedList indexed reads traverse nodes and have poorer locality. Once a linked-list iterator is positioned, insertion there can be constant time. Finding the position still costs traversal, while ArrayList may need to shift elements.
3-05: Overloading means several methods share a name but have different parameter lists. The compiler picks an overload using declared argument types. Overriding replaces an inherited instance method with the same signature. For Animal a = new Dog(), a.speak() calls Dog's overridden method at runtime.
3-06: An abstract class can store instance fields, define constructors and provide shared implementations. An interface specifies a contract and can provide default behavior, but its fields are constants and it has no instance constructor. A Java class extends one superclass and may implement multiple interfaces.
3-07: A final reference can be assigned only once. It cannot be redirected to a different object, but it does not freeze that object. If a final variable holds an ArrayList, calling its add method can still change the list. Use an immutable collection or defensive copy when contents must not change.
3-08: A String's character content cannot change after construction, which makes sharing and interning safe and makes the value suitable as a stable key. Repeatedly concatenating in a loop can repeatedly copy earlier content. StringBuilder accumulates text in a mutable buffer and converts it to a String at the end.
3-09: Checked exceptions such as IOException must be caught or declared by methods that can propagate them. Unchecked exceptions such as IllegalArgumentException are not subject to that rule. Catch an exception where you can recover or add useful context. Declaring a checked exception can be the right way to hand responsibility to the caller.
3-10: Try-with-resources calls close on each successfully initialized AutoCloseable when the block exits, including by exception. Resources close in reverse initialization order. If the block throws and closing throws too, the block exception remains primary and the close exception is available as a suppressed exception.
3-11: `List<String>` tells the compiler that elements must be strings, so it rejects adding an integer and avoids manual casts when reading. A raw `List` loses those checks. Type erasure means generic type arguments generally do not create distinct runtime classes, though the compiler still enforces their types in source.
3-12: If a `List<Integer>` could be assigned to a `List<Number>` variable, code using that variable could add a Double. The original list would then contain something other than an Integer. Java makes these generic types invariant to prevent this. Use a wildcard when a more flexible access pattern is appropriate.
3-13: Use `List<? extends Number>` to read numbers from a list whose exact element subtype is unknown. You cannot safely add a non-null Number to it. Use `List<? super Integer>` to add Integer values into a compatible list. Reading from the latter only guarantees Object without additional checks.
3-14: A record is a special class for a named set of components. It provides component accessors, a canonical constructor, equals, hashCode and toString. Component references are final, but if one references a mutable List, the list can still change. A defensive immutable copy protects the record's value from outside mutation.
3-15: A static method belongs to the class, needs no instance and cannot directly read instance fields. It makes sense for operations such as converting units or constructing a value from arguments. If an operation depends on a particular object's state, an instance method usually makes that dependency clear.
3-16: Incrementing a shared counter involves reading, adding and writing. If two threads interleave those steps, both can read the same value and one update is lost. Synchronizing both increments on the same monitor prevents the interleaving. Unlocking and later locking that monitor also establishes visibility for protected state.
3-17: Volatile makes reads and writes of the field visible, but count++ is a compound operation. Two threads can both read 5, compute 6 and store 6. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet for an atomic increment or guard the full read-modify-write sequence with the same lock.
3-18: An ExecutorService accepts tasks and schedules them on workers. A fixed thread pool can reuse workers instead of creating a new thread per task, and submit can return a Future for a result or failure. Shut it down when finished so it stops accepting tasks and its workers can terminate.
3-19: Optional communicates that a method may have no result, such as a lookup with no match. Return Optional.empty for absence and use map, orElse, orElseGet or orElseThrow at the call site. Calling get on an empty Optional throws, so a caller should decide explicitly what absence means.
3-20: Intermediate operations such as filter describe lazy processing. A terminal operation such as count consumes the pipeline, so reusing that Stream is invalid. To process a reusable collection twice, create two streams by calling collection.stream separately, or combine work into one traversal when that makes sense.
4-01: A process typically has its own virtual address space and resource handles. A thread is an execution path with its own registers, program counter and stack. Threads in the same process share the address space and many process resources, so they can share data directly and may need synchronization.
4-02: The operating system saves the running thread's execution context, including registers and the instruction pointer, and restores another thread's context. The scheduler and save/restore work take time. Switching address spaces or disrupting caches and translation caches can add overhead before useful execution resumes.
4-03: Round robin gives each runnable job a time slice and requeues it if it is still runnable. A shorter quantum can improve interactive response but spends a larger fraction of time on context switches. A very long quantum reduces switches but approaches first-come, first-served behavior.
4-04: If higher-priority jobs keep arriving, a low-priority job may never get the CPU. Aging raises a waiting job's effective priority as its wait grows. Eventually it can compete with newer high-priority work, reducing starvation under the scheduler's rules.
4-05: A regular function call transfers control within the same privilege level. A system call enters the kernel through a defined CPU mechanism, where arguments and permissions are checked before a privileged service such as opening a file. The kernel returns to user mode with a result or error.
4-06: Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames. A page table maps virtual page numbers to frames and records access permissions. The page offset stays unchanged during translation. Fixed-size frames allow neighboring virtual pages to occupy nonadjacent physical frames.
4-07: A page fault occurs when the CPU cannot complete a memory access through the current page mapping or permissions. The kernel may allocate or load a valid missing page and retry the instruction. For an unmapped or forbidden access it can signal an error such as a segmentation fault. Not every page fault reads disk.
4-08: A translation lookaside buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical page translations and related permissions. A hit can avoid a page-table walk on a memory access. A miss requires finding the mapping in the page table. A TLB miss alone does not imply the page is absent from memory.
4-09: Internal fragmentation wastes space inside an allocated unit, such as a 4 KiB page with only 3 KiB of useful data. External fragmentation splits free space into separated gaps, such as two free 4 KiB gaps that cannot satisfy one contiguous 8 KiB request.
4-10: FIFO evicts the oldest resident page, so adding frames can change the eviction order and produce more misses for some reference sequences. In ideal LRU, the pages kept with k frames are always a subset of those kept with k+1 frames. Every hit with k frames remains a hit with k+1.
4-11: Thrashing happens when active processes cannot keep enough of their frequently used pages in memory. They repeatedly fault and evict pages needed again soon, so useful computation slows while paging dominates. Giving working sets more frames or reducing the number of active processes can help.
4-12: A mutex protects a critical section by allowing one holder at a time, usually with ownership rules. Use it around a shared list update. A counting semaphore tracks permits, so five permits can represent five available resources. Tasks acquire one permit before using a resource and release it afterward.
4-13: If two threads update a shared balance by reading, adding and writing, their steps can overlap and lose an update. A critical section groups the steps that must appear indivisible. A common mutex or atomic operation ensures that other updates cannot observe or overwrite an incomplete state.
4-14: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. To break circular wait, assign locks a total order and require every thread to acquire them in that order. Then a wait cycle would require some thread to acquire a lock out of order.
4-15: In deadlock, tasks wait indefinitely on dependencies such as locks held by one another. In livelock, tasks keep changing state but still do not finish, as when both participants repeatedly back off and retry in lockstep. Randomized or coordinated backoff can help break that symmetry.
4-16: Producers put items into a bounded buffer and wait while it is full. Consumers take items and wait while it is empty. A mutex protects buffer state, with condition variables for not-full and not-empty, or counting semaphores for empty and filled slots. An awakened thread checks its condition again.
4-17: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode. Removing one name leaves the file accessible through remaining links. A symbolic link stores a target path, so deleting or moving that target can leave a dangling link. Symlinks can point across filesystems, unlike ordinary hard links.
4-18: Unlink removes a directory entry. An open file descriptor still refers to the file, so the process can continue reading or writing it. The filesystem can reclaim its space when the link count reaches zero and the final open reference is released.
4-19: A zombie is an exited child whose termination status has not yet been collected by its parent. An orphan is a child whose parent has exited first, and it can still be running. On Unix-like systems a designated reaper, such as init or a subreaper, adopts orphans and collects their exit status.
4-20: A journal records intended changes so recovery can replay committed work and ignore or roll back incomplete work after a crash. Metadata journaling records filesystem structure changes, while full data journaling also records file contents. Full data journaling can provide stronger recovery guarantees at the cost of additional writes.
5-01: TCP provides an ordered, reliable byte stream and hides retransmission from the application. Web requests using HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 commonly use it. UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not guarantee delivery or order. Real-time voice can use UDP because a late audio packet may be less useful than continuing playback.
5-02: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number. The server replies with SYN-ACK to acknowledge the client's number and advertise its own. The client ACKs the server. This establishes that both directions work and synchronizes the sequence numbers used for tracking stream bytes.
5-03: TCP numbers stream bytes and acknowledgments tell the sender which bytes have arrived. A gap can produce repeated acknowledgments or selective acknowledgment information. The sender uses these signals and retransmission timers to infer loss, resend missing data and eventually deliver the stream in order.
5-04: Flow control protects the receiver from more data than its buffer can hold, using an advertised receive window. Congestion control limits how much traffic enters the network path, using signals such as loss or delay. The sender must respect both because a fast receiver can still sit behind a congested link.
5-05: Your device's stub resolver asks a recursive resolver for the website name. The recursive resolver answers from cache when possible. Otherwise it follows referrals from root and top-level-domain servers to an authoritative server, gets the relevant record, and caches the response subject to its TTL.
5-06: An A record directly maps a name to an IPv4 address. A CNAME maps an alias to another DNS name. The resolver may need to query that target to get its A or AAAA record, unless it already has the address from cache or the DNS response.
5-07: TTL is the time, in seconds, a DNS answer can be cached. Changing a record does not purge older cache entries everywhere. Resolvers that cached it at different times may continue returning the old value until their remaining TTL expires, while uncached requests can see the new value immediately.
5-08: ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a link-layer address on the local network, such as learning the gateway's MAC address. DNS resolves hostnames to records such as IP addresses. Once DNS gives an IPv4 destination, ARP may still be needed to send the next Ethernet frame.
5-09: A host consults its routing table. For an on-link destination, it sends the frame directly to the peer's MAC address. If a remote destination matches only the default route, it sends the frame to the default gateway's MAC address while keeping the remote destination IP in the packet.
5-10: A /26 leaves six host bits, so blocks contain 64 addresses. The address 192.0.2.70 is in the 192.0.2.64–192.0.2.127 block. Under ordinary subnet conventions, .64 is the network address and .127 is the broadcast address, leaving .65–.126 as 62 usable host addresses.
5-11: Common IPv4 NAT uses address and port translation so multiple internal connections can share a public IP. The gateway keeps mappings to route replies back to the right device. An unsolicited inbound connection usually needs an explicit mapping such as port forwarding, since it has no matching connection state.
5-12: An Ethernet switch forwards frames within a local network using MAC addresses. A router forwards IP packets between networks using a routing table. In an office, a switch can connect the desks within one VLAN, and a router or layer-3 switch can route traffic to other VLANs or the internet.
5-13: A VLAN creates a separate layer-2 broadcast domain on shared switching hardware. For example, guest and staff devices can use the same physical switches while broadcasts stay within their own VLANs. Traffic between VLANs needs layer-3 routing, where access policy can also be applied.
5-14: An Ethernet MTU limits the frame's layer-3 payload, commonly 1500 bytes for a standard link. An IPv4 router may fragment an oversized packet if fragmentation is allowed, or drop it and signal that the path MTU is smaller. IPv6 routers do not fragment and instead send a Packet Too Big message.
5-15: HTTPS runs HTTP over TLS. It encrypts traffic, detects tampering and authenticates the server hostname when certificate validation succeeds. It does not prove a site is trustworthy or protect data after a compromised client or server decrypts it.
5-16: The browser checks that the certificate covers the hostname, is valid, and chains to a trusted issuer under its validation rules. The server proves control of the corresponding private key during the TLS handshake. Together those checks bind the encrypted connection to the requested hostname, not to a judgment of site quality.
5-17: Latency is the delay for data or a response to travel, while bandwidth is capacity per unit of time. A long-distance link can deliver a large file quickly once it is transferring steadily and still feel slow for interactive requests that require multiple round trips.
5-18: A CDN can serve a cached script or image from a nearby edge location, reducing latency and load on the origin. Personalized API responses need cache rules that prevent one user's data being served to another, such as private or no-store directives when appropriate. Public and private assets need different policies.
5-19: HTTP 429 means the request rate exceeded a limit. If Retry-After is present, wait until the specified time or delay has passed. Otherwise follow the API's guidance or use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Immediate repeated retries consume capacity and can keep hitting the same limit.
5-20: A forward proxy represents clients, such as a campus proxy that sends students' outbound web requests. A reverse proxy represents servers, such as a public gateway that accepts requests and routes them to different backend instances. The names describe which side the proxy is deployed on behalf of.
6-01: The derivative at a point is the slope approached by secant lines as their two x-values come together. For f(x)=x², the difference quotient is ((x+h)²−x²)/h=2x+h. Taking h to zero gives f′(x)=2x, so at x=3 the tangent slope is 6.
6-02: Use the chain rule when one function is applied to another. With u=3x+1 and f=u⁴, the outer derivative is 4u³ and the inner derivative is 3. Multiplying gives f′(x)=12(3x+1)³.
6-03: The product rule accounts for both factors changing. For f(x)=x² sin x, the derivative is 2x sin x + x² cos x. Multiplying 2x by cos x would miss the change in each factor weighted by the other factor's original value.
6-04: A definite integral counts area above the horizontal axis positively and area below it negatively. For f(x)=x on [−1,1], the left triangle contributes −1/2 and the right contributes +1/2. The integral is zero even though the total geometric area is 1.
6-05: For continuous f, the accumulated area A(x)=∫ from a to x of f(t) dt has derivative f(x). If F is an antiderivative, the definite integral from a to b is F(b)−F(a). An indefinite integral adds +C because derivatives cannot distinguish antiderivatives that differ by a constant.
6-06: A sequence lists terms, such as 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, whose limit here is zero. A series adds them and studies the limit of the partial sums. In this geometric example, the partial sums approach 1. The terms tending to zero and the sums converging are different statements.
6-07: Group 1/2, then 1/3+1/4, then 1/5 through 1/8, and so on. Each group contains twice as many terms as the previous one and sums to at least 1/2. The partial sums grow without bound. Terms tending to zero are necessary for convergence but do not guarantee it.
6-08: For the matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d), the determinant is ad−bc. If it is zero, the columns are linearly dependent and the matrix is singular. A nonzero determinant guarantees an inverse for this square matrix.
6-09: For a square invertible matrix A, its inverse satisfies A⁻¹A=AA⁻¹=I, where I leaves vectors unchanged. Then Ax=b gives x=A⁻¹b. Rectangular or singular systems may have no solution, many solutions or an approximate solution. Use elimination to check consistency, or least squares when approximation is intended.
6-10: A nonzero eigenvector v satisfies Av=λv. The transformation keeps it on the same line through the origin, with λ describing the scaling and possibly a reversal. For diag(2,3), the x-axis has eigenvalue 2 and the y-axis has eigenvalue 3.
6-11: Rank counts independent columns, equivalently independent rows. For Ax=b, it tells how many independent directions the columns span. The system is consistent when b lies in that span, equivalently when adding b does not increase rank. If a consistent system has fewer pivots than unknowns, it has free variables.
6-12: The dot product is 2×1 + 1×(−2)=0. For nonzero vectors, the dot product equals the product of their lengths times the cosine of the angle, so zero means a right angle. The zero vector has dot product zero with everything but no defined direction.
6-13: Joint probability P(A∩B) is measured over the whole sample space. Conditional probability restricts the sample space to B, so P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) for P(B)>0. For a fair die, even and greater than 3 occurs on 4 and 6, so the joint probability is 2/6, but given greater than 3 it is 2/3.
6-14: If prevalence is 1%, a test with 90% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate gives about 90 true positives and 495 false positives among 10,000 people. Therefore P(condition|positive) is 90/(90+495), about 15%. Bayes' rule combines prevalence and test behavior, so sensitivity alone cannot answer this question.
6-15: A committee ignores order, so there are C(n,3)=n(n−1)(n−2)/6 choices. For chair, secretary and treasurer, assigning the same people to different roles counts separately, so there are n(n−1)(n−2) choices. A combination divides by the number of equivalent orderings.
6-16: In general, P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B|A) when P(A)>0. If the events are independent, P(B|A)=P(B), so the marginals multiply. For two draws without replacement from a deck, the first draw changes the second probability, so use the conditional rule.
6-17: Check n=1: the sum is 1, matching 1×2/2. Assume the first k positive integers sum to k(k+1)/2. Adding k+1 gives (k+1)(k+2)/2. The base case and this implication prove the formula for every positive integer.
6-18: Divide 84 by 30 to get remainder 24. Then 30 mod 24=6 and 24 mod 6=0, so the gcd is 6. A number divides both a and b exactly when it divides both b and a−qb, so replacing a by its remainder preserves the common divisors.
6-19: If x=bᵘ and y=bᵛ, then xy=bᵘ⁺ᵛ, so log_b(xy)=log_b(x)+log_b(y). For real logarithms, x and y must be positive, and the base b must be positive and different from 1.
6-20: Move 5 to the right: x²+6x=−5. Add (6/2)²=9 to both sides to get (x+3)²=4. Thus x+3=±2 and x=−1 or −5. These agree with the roots of (x+1)(x+5)=0.
7-01: HTML provides the form's structure, including labels, inputs and a submit button. CSS controls the layout, spacing and appearance. JavaScript adds behavior, such as sending a sign-in request and showing its result without a full page reload. The server still validates credentials and authorizes actions.
7-02: A native button exposes the button role and can receive focus and respond to Enter or Space by default. A clickable div lacks those behaviors unless they are recreated. Semantic elements communicate intent to both browsers and assistive technology and reduce the work needed for keyboard support.
7-03: Flexbox lays out items primarily along one axis, such as arranging a row of navigation links and distributing space. Grid lets you size and align rows and columns together, such as making cards line up in a two-dimensional gallery. A page can use both for different components.
7-04: A box consists of content, padding, border and outer margin. With content-box, declared width is just the content, so padding and border increase its visible size. With border-box, width includes content, padding and border. Margin stays outside the border box in either model.
7-05: First check the cascade rules, including origin, importance and layer. Among otherwise comparable declarations, specificity favors selectors such as an ID over a class, and later source order breaks ties. Cascade layers are resolved before specificity, so a normal declaration in a later layer can beat a more specific selector in an earlier layer.
7-06: Put one click handler on the list container and let clicks bubble to it. Find the relevant child with `event.target.closest(...)` and check that the match belongs to the container. New list items work automatically because they share the parent listener instead of needing individual listeners.
7-07: Await throws when the awaited promise rejects, so a try/catch can handle network failures. Fetch normally resolves even for HTTP 404 or 500, because a response arrived. Check `response.ok` or its status and handle that case explicitly, such as throwing your own error before reading the success payload.
7-08: Both store strings by origin and can be read by scripts running on that origin. LocalStorage persists across tabs and browser restarts until cleared or restricted. SessionStorage is also scoped to the tab's page session and normally survives reloads but not closing that tab. An XSS bug can expose either.
7-09: GET reads a resource, POST commonly creates a resource or requests an action, PUT replaces a resource at a known URL, and PATCH changes part of it. GET and PUT are idempotent by definition. POST and PATCH need operation-specific guarantees, such as an idempotency key, before ambiguous failures can be retried safely.
7-10: Browsers automatically attach matching cookies, which makes them convenient but requires CSRF protections for sensitive actions. HttpOnly can prevent script access to a cookie. An application can explicitly send a bearer token in the Authorization header. If JavaScript stores or handles it, an XSS bug can steal it, and whoever possesses it can normally use it.
7-11: A cross-origin request using a method such as PUT or a header such as Authorization usually triggers an OPTIONS preflight. The browser checks the server's allowed origins, methods and headers before sending the request. CORS is a browser permission mechanism. The API still needs authentication and authorization for its data.
7-12: XSS occurs when content from a post is interpreted as executable markup, such as an injected event handler. Render plain text as text, or sanitize allowed markup with a well-maintained sanitizer and safe link policies. A strict Content Security Policy can limit damage as a second layer, and input remains untrusted.
7-13: Prepared statements separate the SQL structure from supplied values. For a search, bind the user text to a parameter instead of concatenating it into the query. The database treats quotes or semicolons in that parameter as data. Use a fixed allowlist for SQL identifiers that cannot be bound.
7-14: Anyone can inspect browser JavaScript, network requests and frontend build output. A bundled secret can be copied and reused. Keep privileged API keys in server environment variables. Expose a restricted backend operation that authenticates the user, checks permissions, validates inputs and applies appropriate limits.
7-15: A local variable is recreated when a React component renders and changing it does not schedule a render. State is retained across renders. Calling its setter schedules React to render with the next state. For arrays and objects, return a new value rather than mutating the current state in place.
7-16: Keys let React match list elements between renders, so a reordered item can keep its correct component state. A stable record ID follows the item when another row is added or removed. Array indexes may instead attach state to positions, which can put an edited value or focus on the wrong item.
7-17: An effect is useful for synchronizing with something outside React, such as registering a listener or updating a network subscription. Include the relevant dependencies and clean up the prior subscription. A value computed solely from current props and state can usually be calculated during rendering without an effect or extra state.
7-18: Search request A can start before request B but finish afterward. If both update the same results unconditionally, the UI can show stale A. Use an AbortController when starting a new request or track a request ID and ignore results that no longer correspond to the latest input.
7-19: A client router can switch views without requesting a new document. Refreshing or opening a deep link asks the server for that path directly. A static host needs to serve the app's index page for client routes, while excluding API routes and static assets so they keep their normal handling.
7-20: Distinguish first loading from a successful empty result. Show a clear error and retry action for recoverable failures. During a refresh, preserve existing useful results where possible and label them as updating instead of blanking the screen. Guard against older responses replacing newer results.
8-01: Speed is the magnitude of velocity. In uniform circular motion the magnitude stays constant, but the velocity direction changes continuously. That change gives an acceleration toward the center of magnitude v²/r, perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.
8-02: Distance counts the length of the path, so it is 60+20=80 metres. Displacement measures the final position relative to the starting point and includes direction. Taking east as positive, the displacement is +60−20=+40 metres, or 40 metres east.
8-03: In an elevator accelerating upward with acceleration a, the floor pushes up with normal force N and gravity pulls down with weight mg. Newton's second law gives N−mg=ma, so N=m(g+a). The normal force equals the weight only when the net vertical acceleration is zero in this setup.
8-04: Isolate the chosen object and draw only external forces acting on it, such as gravity, normal contact, tension or friction. Choose convenient axes and resolve forces into components. Do not draw the equal and opposite forces that the object exerts on other bodies or count components as additional forces.
8-05: Static friction adjusts to oppose impending relative motion, up to a maximum typically modeled as μₛN. A small horizontal push on a stationary box may require only a small opposing force. Once sliding starts, kinetic friction is often modeled as roughly μₖN and points opposite the relative sliding velocity.
8-06: Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential energy. It stays constant when only conservative forces do work and no energy crosses the system boundary as mechanical work. Kinetic friction can convert mechanical energy into thermal energy, reducing the mechanical total while total energy is still conserved for an appropriately defined system.
8-07: If external impulse is negligible, the total momentum before and after the collision is the same because internal impulses cancel in pairs. In an inelastic collision, some initial kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat or sound. Momentum conservation does not require kinetic energy conservation.
8-08: Work transfers energy through a force acting over a displacement. Lifting the same mass through the same height at steady speed gives each person work mgh against gravity. Average power is work divided by time, so the person who lifts it faster delivers more power.
8-09: Torque depends on the chosen pivot and equals force times its perpendicular lever arm. A push perpendicular to the door farther from the hinge produces more torque than an equal push near it. A force whose line of action passes through the hinge gives zero torque about that hinge.
8-10: A deeper point supports the weight of more liquid above it. For a stationary liquid of constant density ρ, pressure at depth h is surface pressure plus ρgh. Greater density, gravity or depth increases the pressure difference. Container shape does not enter this relation.
8-11: Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. A floating object settles at a depth where it displaces enough fluid for buoyancy to equal its weight. If even full submersion cannot displace fluid equal in weight to the object, its weight exceeds the maximum buoyant force and it sinks.
8-12: In a resistive wire, the electric field supplies energy to moving charges, which transfer it to the material through scattering. The wire dissipates power P=IV=I²R for resistance R. Much of that energy appears as heat and is then transferred to the surroundings.
8-13: Voltage is energy transferred per unit charge, measured in joules per coulomb. Current is charge flow per unit time, measured in coulombs per second. In a battery-resistor circuit, voltage drives current, and for an ohmic resistor the relationship is I=V/R.
8-14: Parallel branches all see the same voltage. Each branch adds its own current to the total, so the circuit draws more current at that voltage than a single branch alone. Since equivalent resistance is voltage divided by total current, it is less than the smallest finite positive branch resistance.
8-15: Place an object beyond the focal length of a converging lens. A ray parallel to the optical axis refracts through the far focus, while a ray through the thin lens's center travels approximately straight. The rays meet on the far side to form a real, inverted image that can be projected on a screen.
8-16: Light travels at different speeds in materials with different refractive indices. At an oblique boundary its direction changes according to Snell's law. Entering a higher refractive index bends it toward the normal, while entering a lower one bends it away when transmission occurs. At normal incidence there is no change in direction.
8-17: In a transverse wave, the disturbance is perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel, as when a horizontal string moves up and down. In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate parallel to the travel direction, as in the compressions and rarefactions of sound in air.
8-18: Two waves of equal frequency and amplitude traveling in opposite directions can interfere to produce a standing wave. At nodes their displacements always cancel, so motion is zero. At antinodes the oscillation amplitude is largest. Fixed ends on a string are nodes.
8-19: Temperature describes thermal state and is related to average particle energy in simple models. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A small hot cup can have a higher temperature than a large warm container even though the larger amount of material can transfer more energy while cooling by a comparable amount.
8-20: Use the convention that Q is positive for heat added to the system and W is positive for work done by the system. Then ΔU=Q−W. Heating increases internal energy unless offset by work leaving, while compressing the system gives negative W and adds energy.
9-01: The mean adds all five values and divides by five, giving 114/5=22.8. The median is the middle ordered value, 4. Moving the largest value even higher would raise the mean but leave the median unchanged, so the median better describes a typical value in this example.
9-02: Variance measures average squared deviation from the mean, with an adjustment when estimating it from a sample. Standard deviation is its square root, in the original units. Both [4,6] and [0,10] average 5, but the second pair lies farther from 5 and has larger variance and standard deviation.
9-03: For independent draws from the same population, deviations from the sample mean must sum to zero, leaving n−1 freely varying deviations. Fitting that mean makes the sum of squared deviations smaller on average than using the true mean. Dividing by n−1 instead of n makes the usual sample variance unbiased.
9-04: The interquartile range is Q3−Q1, the distance from the 25th to the 75th percentile. It describes the spread of the middle half of the values. Since a few extreme values do not usually move the quartiles much, it is useful alongside the median for skewed data.
9-05: The line inside the box marks the median. The edges mark Q1 and Q3. In a Tukey box plot, the whiskers extend to the most extreme observed values within 1.5 IQR of the box and points beyond are drawn separately. Other plots can use the minimum and maximum or another convention, so check the legend.
9-06: A histogram groups numeric data into adjacent intervals and shows their distribution. A bar chart displays separate categories with bar heights representing quantities. Changing histogram bin widths or boundaries can reveal or hide features, and with unequal widths the area, rather than raw height, should represent frequency.
9-07: Ice cream sales and swimming can rise together because both increase in hot weather. Their correlation does not establish that either causes the other. Stronger evidence comes from a well-designed randomized experiment when feasible, or a credible observational design that addresses alternative explanations.
9-08: Take x values −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 with y=x². Each positive x and its negative counterpart give the same y, so their contributions to covariance cancel and Pearson correlation is zero. Pearson correlation measures linear association, while this relationship is perfectly predictable and nonlinear.
9-09: A p-value is the probability, under the null model and test assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one in the sense defined by the test. It is calculated assuming the null model, so it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
9-10: A 95% confidence interval procedure would cover the fixed true parameter in 95% of repetitions under its assumptions. Once an interval is calculated, it either contains that parameter or does not. The confidence level describes the procedure's coverage, not a probability assigned to the parameter in this particular interval.
9-11: If the new teaching method has no effect, a Type I error is concluding that it does. If it truly improves results, a Type II error is failing to detect that effect. Power is 1 minus the Type II error probability for a specified true effect and study design.
9-12: A study with thousands of students may detect a 0.2-point improvement with a low p-value, yet that gain may have little educational value. Report the estimated effect, confidence interval, scale, and a threshold for a meaningful change. Statistical evidence and practical importance answer different questions.
9-13: For independent observations with common variance σ², the sample mean has standard error σ/√n. Quadrupling the sample size halves this standard error. Increasing n reduces random sampling variability, but it does not automatically remove bias or account for dependent observations.
9-14: For independent, identically distributed observations with finite, nonzero variance, the standardized sample mean approaches a normal distribution as n grows. The speed of approximation depends on the source distribution. The theorem concerns the distribution of repeated sample means, not the shape of the original observations.
9-15: Before and after scores for the same student form a pair. Analyze the within-student differences with a paired method so the pairing is preserved. Scores from independently sampled groups need an independent-groups method because there is no natural one-to-one correspondence.
9-16: If a class survey reaches only students who attend an optional review session, those students may differ systematically from the class. Selecting students at random from the whole class helps represent it and supports estimates of sampling uncertainty. Poor coverage or selective nonresponse can still cause bias.
9-17: In a study relating tutoring to grades, prior preparation may influence who seeks tutoring and also affect grades. It can confound the observed association. Randomly assigning tutoring tends to balance prior preparation and other baseline factors across groups, making their outcomes more comparable.
9-18: In a linear model, a slope is the expected change in the response for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding other included predictors constant. Its units are response units per predictor unit. Outside the observed range, the relationship may change, so extrapolated predictions can be unreliable.
9-19: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise or peculiarities in training data that do not generalize. It may fit training examples very well while performing poorly on held-out examples. Compare training and validation results using an independent holdout or cross-validation, with preprocessing fitted on the training portion only.
9-20: The true mean grade for all students in a college is a population parameter. The mean grade for a random sample is a sample statistic that estimates it. Different samples produce different estimates, and a standard error or interval can describe that sampling uncertainty under stated assumptions.
10-01: Ohm's law gives V=IR for an ohmic resistor with constant resistance under the operating conditions. Rearranging, I=12 V / 6 Ω=2 A. If heating or another effect changes the resistance substantially, a single constant-R model may no longer describe the device.
10-02: Kirchhoff's current law says that current entering a node equals current leaving it in the usual lumped-circuit model. Kirchhoff's voltage law says that signed voltage rises and drops sum to zero around a closed loop when no unmodeled changing magnetic flux links it. Use consistent reference directions for both.
10-03: Series resistors share the same current because there is no branch between them. Their voltage drops add, so V=I(R1+R2+R3). The equivalent resistance here is 2+3+5=10 Ω.
10-04: Parallel resistors have the same voltage and their branch currents add. The equivalent resistance satisfies 1/R=1/6+1/3=1/2, so R=2 Ω. It is smaller than either branch resistance because the same voltage drives both paths.
10-05: With no output load, the same current flows through both series resistors. The output across the lower resistor is 9 V × 2 kΩ / (1 kΩ + 2 kΩ)=6 V. The ratio of the lower resistance to the total sets that fraction of the source voltage.
10-06: A load from the output to ground is in parallel with the lower resistor. For the 9 V divider with 1 kΩ above and 2 kΩ below, a 2 kΩ load reduces the lower equivalent to 1 kΩ. The output becomes 9 × 1/(1+1)=4.5 V instead of the unloaded 6 V.
10-07: During charging, current flows as the capacitor voltage changes according to i=C dv/dt. After a long time with a stable DC source in a settling circuit, its voltage is constant and ideal current is zero. It then acts like an open circuit while it can retain voltage across its terminals.
10-08: For an ideal inductor, v=L di/dt. A voltage is needed to change its current, so startup behavior depends on the surrounding circuit and initial current. If the circuit reaches a constant current in DC steady state, the voltage across the ideal inductor is zero, like a short circuit.
10-09: The time constant is τ=RC. Here 10,000 Ω × 100×10⁻⁶ F=1 second. For an initially uncharged capacitor in a simple series RC circuit driven by a DC step, its voltage reaches 1−e⁻¹, about 63%, of the final voltage after one time constant.
10-10: A capacitor stores energy in its electric field, with energy ½CV² for capacitance C and voltage V. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field, with energy ½LI² for inductance L and current I. These expressions assume ideal linear components.
10-11: RMS is the square root of the mean of the squared voltage over a cycle. Across a fixed resistor, it equals the DC voltage that produces the same average heating. For a sinusoid, RMS is peak/√2, so a 10 V peak gives about 7.07 V RMS.
10-12: In sinusoidal steady state, real power P is the average rate of energy transfer to the load, in watts. Reactive power Q measures the oscillating exchange associated with electric and magnetic fields, in var. Power factor is P divided by apparent power, and equals the cosine of the voltage-current phase difference in this case.
10-13: An ideal transformer has Vs/Vp=Ns/Np and the inverse current ratio. With twice as many primary turns as secondary turns, the secondary voltage is half the primary voltage and the secondary current is twice the primary current for the same apparent power under load. This assumes AC operation and no losses.
10-14: A diode conducts mainly in the forward direction and blocks reverse current under normal operating conditions. In series with a load, it can pass one polarity of a sinusoidal input and block the other, producing half-wave pulses. A real diode introduces a forward voltage drop.
10-15: A bridge uses four diodes so that two conduct during each half-cycle. The conducting pair changes, but current through the load keeps the same direction. Both halves become positive pulses at twice the input frequency, yet the output still varies between peaks without a filter.
10-16: The capacitor charges near rectified voltage peaks when the source exceeds its voltage. Between peaks the diodes stop conducting and the capacitor supplies the load, so the voltage falls gradually. Larger capacitance, smaller load current or a higher pulse frequency generally reduces the peak-to-peak ripple.
10-17: A fuse opens when excess current heats its element enough to melt it. Correctly rated, it helps protect wiring and equipment against overloads or short circuits. It is a one-time protective device, while a switch is intended for normal control and can be operated repeatedly.
10-18: A linear two-terminal network can be modeled by a Thevenin voltage source Vth in series with Rth, or a Norton current source In in parallel with the same resistance. For finite nonzero Rth, In=Vth/Rth. Both equivalents produce the same terminal voltage and current for the same load.
10-19: For a fixed source modeled by Vth and positive Rth, a resistive load receives maximum power when RL=Rth. At this match, half the power is dissipated inside the source model. Increasing RL improves the fraction delivered to the load, but reduces current and can decrease the actual load power.
10-20: With ideal negative feedback and unsaturated operation, the inverting input is at the same voltage as the grounded non-inverting input. Negligible input current means the current through Rin also flows through Rf, so Vin/Rin=−Vout/Rf. Therefore the voltage gain is −Rf/Rin, and the minus sign indicates inversion.
